messages.subject: CALL FOR NOMINATIONS: 2021 Rohlf Medal
messages.body_plain:
The Rohlf Medal was established in 2006 by the family and friends of F. James Rohlf to mark his 70th birthday. He has been a longtime Stony Brook University faculty member and is currently Emeritus Distinguished Professor in the Department of Ecology and Evolution, and Research Professor in the Department of Anthropology.

Recipients of the Rohlf Medal will be recognized for excellence in their sustained body of work on the development of new morphometric methods or for their applications in the biomedical sciences, including evolutionary biology, population biology, physical anthropology, and medicine. The term "morphometrics" is intended to include high-dimensional pattern analyses of biological shape, especially those that analyse shape in a comprehensive way, or of covariation of shape with other variables. The award can recognize a body of work that has significantly advanced the field, including: mathematical or statistical theory underlying morphometric methods, software that implements or visualizes new methods, or a body of biological findings that rely crucially on contemporary morphometric methods and represent major advances.

Candidates for the Rohlf Medal may be self-nominated or nominated by others. They must possess a Ph.D. degree or the equivalent.

The winning candidate must agree to attend the award ceremony in person in order to accept the Rohlf Medal and then deliver the award lecture.   Note: the event may have to be virtual this year due to COVID-19. A decision will be announced later.

Nomination packages should include,

1.     1: a description of the body of work (not to exceed two pages) on which the candidacy is based,

2.     2: reprints of no more than three relevant papers and/or software products,

3.     3: a curriculum vitae, and

4.     4: the names and addresses of three referees.

Nominating packages should be uploaded to the   Rohlf Medal application <http://sbmorphometrics.org/RohlfMedal/nominations/apply.html>  website and received by 5 pm, EST, 15 July 2021  to be assured of full consideration. Note that upon request nominations from 2019 can be retained for the 2021 selection (though updates of some of the information will likely be needed).

The successful candidate will receive the Rohlf Medal and a cash prize at Stony Brook University, planned for on or about   October 24th, 2021. She or he will deliver a lecture that is appropriate for a broad audience, ranging from the exact sciences to the humanities, concerning the morphometric methodology, software, or findings for which the Rohlf Medal was awarded.

If you have questions about this nomination or need information, please contact Dean Adams (Chair).

Dean (on behalf of the Rohlf Medal committee)

messages.subject: Help with Trajectory Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear Geomorph Community,

Apologies for this question in advance, it's likely a really simple fix and probably a basic error on my part, but I can't for the life of me seem to fix it.

I'm trying to look at conducting a trajectory analysis to look at potential convergent morphology in a pair of morphologically similar snail species, comparing historical museum individuals to contemporary populations. The contemporary populations appear to have more overlapping morphologies than historical indv., but I'm trying to work out if this is through converging of shape, or an artefact reduction in population sizes.

I have a dataset of 13 LMs for 162 individuals, with X and Y coords for each LM. I'm loading a TPS file with these to use in the trajectory analysis. I'm using the code below, but when I get to the lm.rrpp step I get the error:

Error: Data are arranged in an array rather than a matrix.
         Please convert data to a matrix.

Am I just using the wrong type of data here for the coordinate data, or making another issue somewhere? Apologies if this is a super basic issue , I just can't seem to get my head around it!

Thanks in advance for your help.

###Reading LM File and Classifiers###
Crass_Uni_All<-readland.tps("crassula_uniplicata_all_topotypes_contemporary_mirrored_LM_scale.tps", specID="imageID", warnmsg=T)
Crass_Uni_Classifier< read.csv("crassula_uniplicata_all_topotypes_contemporary_classifier.csv")

###Running GPA on LM data
Crass_Uni_All.gpa<-gpagen(Crass_Uni_All)

###Building Data Frame of GPA Data and Species + Type Variables###
Crass_Uni_All.gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(coords=Crass_Uni_All.gpa$coords, species = Crass_Uni_Classifier$Species, type = Crass_Uni_Classifier$Type)

###Developing Model for Trajectory Analysis###
fit <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ Species * Type, data = Crass_Uni_All.gdf, iter = 199)
reveal.model.designs(fit)

###Trajectory Analysis Using Model###
Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory<- trajectory.analysis(fit, groups=Crass_Uni_All$species,
                                               traj.pts= Crass_Uni_All$Type, print.progress=FALSE)

# Magnitude difference (absolute difference between path distances)
summary(Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory, attribute = "MD")

# Correlations (angles) between trajectories
summary(Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory, attribute = "TC", angle.type = "deg")

# No shape differences between vectors
summary(Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory, attribute = "SD")

# Retain results
Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory.summary <- summary(Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory, attribute = "MD")
Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory.summary$summary.table

# Plot results
TrajPlot <- plot(Crass_Uni_All_Trajectory, pch = as.numeric(Crass_Uni_All$Type) + 20, bg = as.numeric(Pupfish$Species),
           cex = 0.7, col = "gray")
add.trajectories(TrajPlot, traj.pch = c(21, 22), start.bg <http://start.bg> = 1, end.bg <http://end.bg> = 2)
legend("topright", levels(Crass_Uni_All$Type), pch =  c(21, 22), pt.bg <http://pt.bg> = 1)

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Nadja,

There are multiple ways to do this, depending on your analytical pipeline.

For instance, if you have multiple specimens per group, one could perform a linear model using ‘procD.lm’, followed by ‘pairwise’. In the output from pairwise, the first component of the LS.means contains these  (e.g., PW.output$LS.means[[1]] ).

If you look at the help file for procD.lm there is an example of both the anova and the pairwise tests.

This is one of many ways to obtain them.

Any phylogenetic comparative method requires that the implementation ‘knows’ which observation corresponds with which tip of the phylogeny. That is based on specimen names matching phylogeny tip names.

data("plethspecies")

new <- combine.subsets(plethspecies$land[1:5,,], plethspecies$land[6:11,,])

new$coords

dimnames(new$coords)[3] <- dimnames(plethspecies$land)[3]

new$coords

Since you have sample imbalances across your species, and you want your PCA shape not to be biased towards species with more samples, an easier solution would be fitting GPA (without scaling) for each species individually, and feeding the consensus shapes from those into your final shape analysis and PCA decomposition. Bob,

As per my paper, CR values less than 1.0 indicate modular signal. However, values greater than 1.0 do NOT represent integration. This is discussed clearly in the paper: the CR is for modularity only (PLS is for integration).

As to your distribution, this is not unexpected. The distribution of CR values obtained via permutation will be ‘tighter’ around 1.0 as the number of landmarks increases. See simulation example below with randomly generated data.

Dean

y <- matrix(rnorm(100000),ncol=500)

gps <- gl(2,250)

res <- modularity.test(y,gps)

plot(res)
